28-Nov-2018: I’ve added a small update at the end on how to prevent ‘handle collisions’ with a per-slot generation counter
Original Post:
…wherein I talk a bit about how I’m doing dynamic memory management in C and C++ these days which basically replaces raw- and smart-pointers with ‘index-handles’.
In my last blog post I was mentioning pointer- and allocation-free programming, but was skipping over the details. This is what the following blog post is about.
This is all based on the (sometimes painful) experience of wrestling for 15+ years with fairly big C++ code bases (0.5 to around 1 mloc) where memory is often managed through smart pointers. The worst case being tens- to hundreds-of-thousands of small C++ objects, each in its own heap allocation, pointing to each other through smart pointers. While such code is quite robust in terms of memory corruption (segfaults and corruption rarely happens, since most attempts are caught by asserts when dereferencing smart pointers), this type of ‘object spiderweb code’ is also dog-slow without obvious starting points for optimization, since the entire code is full of cache misses. Other typical problems are memory fragmentation and ‘fake memory leaks’ because a forgotten smart pointer prevents freeing the underlying memory (I call them ‘fake leaks’ because this type of leaks cannot be caught by memory debugging tools).
Nothing presented here is particularly new or clever, it’s just a collection of a few simple ideas which together work fairly well in bigger code bases to prevent (or at least detect early) a number of common memory-related problems in C and C++, and may even be useful in higher-level garbage-collected languages to reduce pressure on the garbage collector.
However, the underlying design philosophy doesn’t fit very well into a classical OOP world where applications are built from small autonomous objects interacting with each other. That’s why it’s also quite tricky to implement those ideas in a big existing OOP code base, where object creation and destruction happens ‘decentralized’ all over the code.
The approach described here works very well though with a data-oriented architecture, where central systems work on arrays of data items packed tightly in memory.
Most of the following blog post is written from a game developer’s perspective, but should also apply to other areas where a program needs to juggle a few hundred to a few million objects (or generally ‘data items’) in memory, and where such items are created and destroyed frequently.
The gist is:
- move all memory management into centralized systems (like rendering, physics, animation, …), with the systems being the sole owner of their memory allocations
- group items of the same type into arrays, and treat the array base pointer as system-private
- when creating an item, only return an ‘index-handle’ to the outside world, not a pointer to the item
- in the index-handles, only use as many bits as needed for the array index, and use the remaining bits for additional memory safety checks
- only convert a handle to a pointer when absolutely needed, and don’t store the pointer anywhere
I’ll explain each of those points in detail below. But the idea is basically that common ‘user-level’ code doesn’t directly call memory allocation functions (like malloc, new or make_shared/make_unique), and reduces the use of pointers to an absolute minimum (only as short-lived references when direct memory access to an item is absolutely needed). Most importantly, pointers are never the ‘owner’ of an item’s underlying memory.
Instead, direct memory manipulation happens as much as possible inside a few centralized systems where memory-related problems are easier to debug and optimize.
Move memory management into central systems
In this blog post, a ‘system’ is a (usually fairly big) part of a code base which takes care of a number of related tasks, like ‘rendering’, ‘physics’, ‘AI’, ‘character animation’ and so on. Such a system is separated from other systems and ‘user-code’ through a clearly defined function API, and the work that happens on the system’s data is performed in tight central loops instead of being spread out all over the code base.
Systems often work on items created and destroyed under control of user code (but note that creation and destruction of items is different from allocating and freeing the memory used by those items!). For instance a rendering system might deal with vertex buffers, textures, shaders and pipeline state objects. A physics system works with rigid bodies, joints and collision primitives, and an animation system works with animation keys and curves.
It makes sense to move the memory management for such items into the systems themselves, because a general memory allocator doesn’t have the system-specific ‘domain knowledge’ about how data items are processed and the relationships between data items. This allows the system to optimize memory allocations, perform additional validation checks when creating and destroying items, and arrange items in memory for making best use of the CPU’s data caches.
A good example for this ‘system domain knowledge’ is the destruction of rendering resource objects with modern 3D APIs: a resource object can not simply be destroyed immediately when the user code says so because the resource might still be referenced in a command list waiting to be consumed by the GPU. Instead the rendering system would only mark the resource object for destruction when the user code requests its destruction, but the actual destruction happens at a later time when the GPU no longer uses the resource.
Group items of the same type into arrays
Once all memory management has moved into systems, the system can optimize memory allocations and memory layout with its additional knowledge about how items are used. One obvious optimization is to reduce the number of general memory allocations by grouping items of the same type into arrays, and allocate those arrays at system startup.
Instead of performing a memory allocation each time a new item is created, the system keeps track of free array slots, and picks the next free slot. When the user code no longer needs the item, the system simply marks the slot as free again instead of performing a deallocation (not different from a typical pool allocator).
This pool allocation is most likely a little bit faster than performing a memory allocation per item, but this is not even the main reason for keeping items in arrays (modern general allocators are quite fast too for small allocations).
A few additional advantages are:
- items are guaranteed to be packed tightly in memory, general allocators sometimes need to keep some housekeeping data next to the actual item memory
- it’s easier to keep ‘hot items’ in continuous memory ranges, so that the CPU can make better use of its data caches
- it’s also possible to split the data of a single item into several subitems in different arrays for even tighter packing and better data cache usage (AoS vs SoA and everything inbetween), and all those data layout details remain private to the system and are trivial to change without affecting ‘outside code’
- as long as the system doesn’t need to reallocate arrays, it is guaranteed that there will be no memory fragmentation (although this is less of an issue in a 64-bit address space)
- it’s easier to detect memory leaks early, and provide more useful error messages: when a new item is created a system can trivially check the current number of items against an expected upper bound (for instance a game might know that there should never be more than 1024 textures alive at a time, and since all textures are created through the rendering system, the system can print out a more useful warning message when this number is exceeded)
Public index-handles instead of pointers
Keeping system items in arrays instead of unique allocations has the advantage that an item can be identified through an array index instead of requiring a full pointer. This is very useful for memory safety. Instead of handing memory pointers to the outside world, the system can treat the array base pointers as ‘private knowledge’, and only hand out array indices to the public. Without the base pointer to compute an item’s memory location, the outside code can’t access the item’s memory, even with a lot of criminal energy.
This has a number of further advantages:
- In many situations, code outside the system never even needs to directly access memory of an item, only the system does. In such an ‘ideal’ situation, user code never accesses memory through pointers, and can never cause memory corruption.
- Since only the system knows the array base pointers, it’s free to move or reallocate the item arrays at will without invalidating existing index handles.
- Array indices need fewer bits than full pointers, and a smaller data type can be picked for them, which in turn allows tighter packing of data structures and better data cache usage (this has the caveat that additional handle bits can be used to increase memory safety, more about this below)
If user code needs to access the memory of an item directly it needs to obtain a pointer through a ‘lookup function’ which takes a handle as input and returns a pointer. As soon as such a lookup function exists, the fairly watertight memory safety scenario outlined above is no longer guaranteed, and the user code should adhere to a few rules:
- pointers should never be stored anywhere, since the next time the pointer is used it may no longer point to the same item, or even to valid memory
- a pointer should only be used in a simple code block, and not ‘across’ function calls
Every time a handle is converted into a pointer, the system can guarantee that the returned pointer still points to the same item that the handle was originally created for (more on this below), but this guarantee ‘decays’ over time since the item under the pointer may have been destroyed, or the underlying memory may have been reallocated to a different location (this is the same problem as iterator invalidation in C++).
The two simple rules above are easy to memorize and are a good compromise between not exposing pointers to user code at all, and having a (somewhat costly) handle-to-pointer conversion for every single memory access.
Memory safety considerations
First, each type of handle should get its own C/C++ type, so that attempting to pass the wrong handle type to a function is already detected at compile time (note that a simple typedef isn’t enough to produce a compiler warning, the handle must be wrapped into its own struct or class - however this could be limited to debug compilation mode).
All runtime memory safety checks happen in the function which converts a handle into a pointer. If the handle is just an array index, it would look like this:
- a range check happens for the index against the current item array size, this prevents segmentation faults and reading or writing allocated but unrelated memory areas
- a check needs to happen whether the indexed array item slot contains an active item (is not currently a ‘free slot’), this prevents the simple variant of ‘use after free’
- finally the item pointer is computed from the private array base pointer and public item index
The resulting pointer is safe to use as long as:
- the item array isn’t reallocated
- the indexed item hasn’t been destroyed
Both can only happen inside one of the system’s functions, that’s why the two ‘pointer usage rules’ exist (don’t store pointers, don’t keep pointers across function calls).
There is a pretty big hole in the above use-after-free check though: if we only check if an array slot behind an index-handle contains a valid item, it’s not guaranteed that it is the same item the handle was originally created for. It can happen that the original item was destroyed, and the same array slot was reused for a new item.
This is where the ‘free bits’ in a handle come in: Let’s say our handles are 16-bits, but we only ever need 1024 items alive at the same time. Only 10 index bits are needed to address 1024 items, which leaves 6 bits free for something else.
If those 6 bits contain some sort of ‘unique pattern’, it’s possible to detect dangling accesses:
- When an item is created, a free array item is picked and its index is put into the lower 10 handle bits. The upper 6 bits are set to a ‘unique bit pattern’
- The resulting 16-bit handle (10 bits index + 6 bit ‘unique pattern’) are returned to the outside world, and at the same time stored with the array slot.
- When an item is destroyed, the item handle stored with the array slot is set to the ‘invalid handle’ value (can be zero, as long as zero is never returned as a valid handle to the outside world)
- When the handle is converted to a pointer, the lower 10 bits are used as array index to lookup the array slot, and the entire 16-bit handle is compared against the handle that’s currently stored with the array slot:
    
  - if both handles are equal, the pointer is valid and points to the same item the handle was created for
  - otherwise this is a dangling access, the slot item has either been destroyed (in that case the stored handle would have the ‘invalid handle’ value), or has been destroyed and reused for a new item (in that case the upper 6 ‘unique pattern’ bits don’t match)
This handle-comparison check when converting a handle to a pointer works quite well to detect dangling-accesses, but it isn’t waterproof because the same combination of array index and ‘unique pattern’ will be created sooner or later. But it’s still better than no dangling protection at all (like raw pointers), or a ‘fake memory leak’ which would happen in similar situations with smart pointers.
Finding good strategies to create unique handles that collide as rarely as possible is the most important part of course, and left as an excercise to the reader ;P
Obviously it’s good to use as many bits for the unique pattern as possible, and the way how free array slots are reused is important as well (e.g. LIFO vs FIFO). It’s probably also good to write a little creation/destruction stress-test which checks for handle collisions and can be used to tweak the unique-pattern creation for specific use cases. A system where items are created and destroyed with a very high frequency needs more effort (or simply more handle bits) than systems where item creation and destruction is a rare occurance.
Other useful properties of handles
Apart from the whole memory safety aspect, handles are also useful for other situations where pointers are problematic:
Handles can be used as shared object identifiers across processes (all you need is some sort of ‘create_item_with_handle()’ function, which doesn’t create a new handle, but takes an existing handle as input argument). This is especially useful for online games where handles can be shared between the server and all clients in a game session, or in savegame systems to store references to other objects.
Sometimes it’s useful to create a whole group of related items (for instance animation keys and curves), and reference the whole item group with a single handle. In that case some sort of ‘range handle’ can be used, which contains not only an index (of the first item), but also the number of items in the range.
In some situations it’s also useful to reserve a few handle bits for an item type if static type checking at compile time isn’t sufficient.
In conclusion, I find it quite surprising how naturally and elegantly handles solve many problems I encountered in the past with the traditional ‘pointers to objects on the heap’ model, and how little I miss this model now (and the parts of C++ that are built around it).

fields.description: macOS ships a VulgarWordUsage.db and a dictionary that rates every word as vulgar, offensive or sensitive. I dumped it for 199,000 English words and a dozen other languages.
fields.text:
TL;DR
- ~/Library/Keyboard/VulgarWordUsage.db is real. It records which swear words you use, per app and per
recipient, so autocorrect learns to stop "ducking" you. On my Mac it is empty, and typing swear words into a native
app did not fill it.
- The interesting part is upstream. Apple's system dictionary flags every word with one of three tiers (vulgar, offensive, sensitive) and up to eleven topic flags (sex, drugs, religion, politics, violence, …).
- There is no public API for any of it. I read the flags with a few private C functions from Lexicon.framework.
Code below, in C and in Swift. The full dumps for 15 languages are in

Where the word list lives
Searching the dyld shared cache for "vulgar" turned up a C API with an LX prefix
(LXVulgarWordUsageDatabaseCreate, LXVulgarWordUsageDatabaseCanAutocorrect, …) and, more usefully, two functions on
dictionary entries:
_LXEntryGetCategoryFlags
_LXEntryGetMetaFlags
LX is Lexicon.framework, a private framework that reads the per-language dictionaries under
/System/Library/LinguisticData/. Every word in those dictionaries is an LXEntry with two 32-bit flag fields. If the
vulgarity rating is anywhere, it's in those bits.
There is no public API
I looked. NSSpellChecker, UITextChecker, NaturalLanguage and UILexicon don't expose vulgarity.
SensitiveContentAnalysis covers images and video, not text. The only places "profanity" shows up on
developer.apple.com are App Store age ratings and review guidelines.
So: private functions. Lexicon has no headers, but the C functions are exported, and their signatures are easy to guess because they follow CoreFoundation conventions. This program opens the dictionary for a locale, walks every entry, and prints both flag fields:
// lx.c — dump every word in a system lexicon with its flags.
// clang -O1 -o lx lx.c -F/System/Library/PrivateFrameworks -framework Lexicon -framework CoreFoundation
#include <CoreFoundation/CoreFoundation.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdio.h>
typedef const void *LXLexiconRef, *LXCursorRef, *LXEntryRef;
extern CFStringRef kLXLexiconLocaleKey;
LXLexiconRef LXLexiconCreate(CFDictionaryRef options, CFErrorRef *error);
LXCursorRef  LXLexiconCreateRootCursor(LXLexiconRef);
void         LXCursorEnumerateEntriesRecursively(LXCursorRef, void (^)(LXEntryRef, bool *stop));
CFStringRef  LXEntryCopyString(LXEntryRef);
uint32_t     LXEntryGetCategoryFlags(LXEntryRef);
uint32_t     LXEntryGetMetaFlags(LXEntryRef);
int main(int argc, char **argv) {
  CFStringRef locale = CFStringCreateWithCString(NULL, argc > 1 ? argv[1] : "en_US", kCFStringEncodingUTF8);
  const void *keys[] = {kLXLexiconLocaleKey}, *values[] = {locale};
  CFDictionaryRef options = CFDictionaryCreate(NULL, keys, values, 1, &kCFTypeDictionaryKeyCallBacks,
                                               &kCFTypeDictionaryValueCallBacks);
  LXLexiconRef lexicon = LXLexiconCreate(options, NULL);
  if (!lexicon) return 1;
  LXCursorEnumerateEntriesRecursively(LXLexiconCreateRootCursor(lexicon), ^(LXEntryRef entry, bool *stop) {
    char word[512] = "";
    CFStringRef s = LXEntryCopyString(entry);
    if (s) { CFStringGetCString(s, word, sizeof word, kCFStringEncodingUTF8); CFRelease(s); }
    printf("%08x\t%08x\t%s\n", LXEntryGetCategoryFlags(entry), LXEntryGetMetaFlags(entry), word);
  });
}

The same thing in Swift, loading the functions at runtime with dlopen and dlsym so you don't need to link against
a private framework. It prints only words that carry one of the three tiers:
// lexflags.swift — swiftc -O lexflags.swift -o lexflags && ./lexflags en_US
import Foundation
let lexicon = dlopen("/System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/Lexicon.framework/Lexicon", RTLD_NOW)!
func sym<T>(_ name: String, as _: T.Type) -> T { unsafeBitCast(dlsym(lexicon, name)!, to: T.self) }
typealias LXRef = UnsafeRawPointer
let create     = sym("LXLexiconCreate", as: (@convention(c) (CFDictionary, UnsafeMutablePointer<Unmanaged<CFError>?>?) -> LXRef?).self)
let rootCursor = sym("LXLexiconCreateRootCursor", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> LXRef?).self)
let enumerate  = sym("LXCursorEnumerateEntriesRecursively", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef, @convention(block) (LXRef, UnsafeMutablePointer<Bool>) -> Void) -> Void).self)
let copyString = sym("LXEntryCopyString", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> Unmanaged<CFString>?).self)
let metaFlags  = sym("LXEntryGetMetaFlags", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> UInt32).self)
let category   = sym("LXEntryGetCategoryFlags", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> UInt32).self)
let localeKey  = dlsym(lexicon, "kLXLexiconLocaleKey")!.load(as: CFString.self)
let locale = CommandLine.arguments.dropFirst().first ?? "en_US"
guard let lex = create([localeKey: locale] as CFDictionary, nil), let root = rootCursor(lex) else {
    fatalError("could not open lexicon for \(locale)")
}
let tiers: [(UInt32, String)] = [(0x0080_0000, "vulgar"), (0x0100_0000, "offensive"), (0x0200_0000, "sensitive")]
enumerate(root) { entry, _ in
    let meta = metaFlags(entry)
    guard let tier = tiers.first(where: { meta & $0.0 != 0 })?.1,
          let word = copyString(entry)?.takeRetainedValue() else { return }
    print(tier, String(format: "%05x", category(entry)), word, separator: "\t")
}

The three tiers (meta flags)
| Bit | Tier | en_US words | Examples | 
|---|---|---|---|
| 0x00800000 | vulgar | 1,050 | fuck, shit, cunt, cock, crap, wtf, fml, bullshitting, fucktard, shizzle, merde |

There is a second, separate filter. Every English language model has a blocklist.bundle, and there's a
qp_blocklist.bundle for QuickPath, the swipe keyboard:
/System/Library/LinguisticData/RequiredAssets_en.bundle/AssetData/en.lm/
├── blocklist.bundle/{blocklist.dat, blocklistidmap.dat}
└── qp_blocklist.bundle/{blocklist.dat, blocklistidmap.dat}
blocklistidmap.dat is a 20-byte header followed by (lexicon token ID, class ID) pairs of 32-bit integers. Mapping
the token IDs back through the dictionary gives 2,544 words in 930 classes. Most classes are inflection groups:
931   fuck | fucked | fucking | fucks
1181  molest | molestation | molested | molester | molesting
1514  died | dies | dying
1611  Holocaust | holocaust | holocausts
1614  denied | denies | deny | denying
923   Semite | Semites | Semitic
1487  ghetto | ghettoes | ghettos
1720  animals | brown | cats
blocklist.dat is a packed trie over those class IDs, so it blocks sequences: "deny" followed by "Holocaust", and
whatever 1720 pairs with. A class that puts brown next to animals and cats suggests the list targets specific
phrasings rather than single words, though which phrasings I can't tell without decoding the trie. The runtime check is LMLanguageModelTokenSequenceIsBlocklisted in
LanguageModeling.framework. I got far enough to learn that its fourth and fifth arguments include an output
pointer, but my probe still crashes intermittently, so I haven't read the actual phrases yet. That's for a follow-up.

- Meanings are inferred. Apple documents none of these bits. The tier names come from an enum in the system code and the topics from reading thousands of samples. Both are consistent, but they're still a reading.
- Flagged is not censored. As far as I can tell these flags decide what the keyboard volunteers, not what you can type.
- One machine. Everything here comes from macOS 15.6 (24G84) with LinguisticData build 438 from July 2025. iOS and other macOS versions may ship different dictionaries.
- Private API. The functions can change or disappear in any update. Don't ship this in an app.

## 

Searching the dyld shared cache for "vulgar" turned up a C API with an `LX` prefix
(`LXVulgarWordUsageDatabaseCreate`, `LXVulgarWordUsageDatabaseCanAutocorrect`, …) and, more usefully, two functions on
dictionary entries:

```
_LXEntryGetCategoryFlags
_LXEntryGetMetaFlags
```
`LX` is `Lexicon.framework`, a private framework that reads the per-language dictionaries under
`/System/Library/LinguisticData/`. Every word in those dictionaries is an `LXEntry` with two 32-bit flag fields. If the
vulgarity rating is anywhere, it's in those bits.

## 

I looked. `NSSpellChecker`, `UITextChecker`, `NaturalLanguage` and `UILexicon` don't expose vulgarity.
`SensitiveContentAnalysis` covers images and video, not text. The only places "profanity" shows up on
developer.apple.com are App Store age ratings and review guidelines.

So: private functions. Lexicon has no headers, but the C functions are exported, and their signatures are easy to guess because they follow CoreFoundation conventions. This program opens the dictionary for a locale, walks every entry, and prints both flag fields:

```
// lx.c — dump every word in a system lexicon with its flags.
// clang -O1 -o lx lx.c -F/System/Library/PrivateFrameworks -framework Lexicon -framework CoreFoundation
#include <CoreFoundation/CoreFoundation.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdio.h>
typedef const void *LXLexiconRef, *LXCursorRef, *LXEntryRef;
extern CFStringRef kLXLexiconLocaleKey;
LXLexiconRef LXLexiconCreate(CFDictionaryRef options, CFErrorRef *error);
LXCursorRef  LXLexiconCreateRootCursor(LXLexiconRef);
void         LXCursorEnumerateEntriesRecursively(LXCursorRef, void (^)(LXEntryRef, bool *stop));
CFStringRef  LXEntryCopyString(LXEntryRef);
uint32_t     LXEntryGetCategoryFlags(LXEntryRef);
uint32_t     LXEntryGetMetaFlags(LXEntryRef);
int main(int argc, char **argv) {
  CFStringRef locale = CFStringCreateWithCString(NULL, argc > 1 ? argv[1] : "en_US", kCFStringEncodingUTF8);
  const void *keys[] = {kLXLexiconLocaleKey}, *values[] = {locale};
  CFDictionaryRef options = CFDictionaryCreate(NULL, keys, values, 1, &kCFTypeDictionaryKeyCallBacks,
                                               &kCFTypeDictionaryValueCallBacks);
  LXLexiconRef lexicon = LXLexiconCreate(options, NULL);
  if (!lexicon) return 1;
  LXCursorEnumerateEntriesRecursively(LXLexiconCreateRootCursor(lexicon), ^(LXEntryRef entry, bool *stop) {
    char word[512] = "";
    CFStringRef s = LXEntryCopyString(entry);
    if (s) { CFStringGetCString(s, word, sizeof word, kCFStringEncodingUTF8); CFRelease(s); }
    printf("%08x\t%08x\t%s\n", LXEntryGetCategoryFlags(entry), LXEntryGetMetaFlags(entry), word);
  });
}
```
```
$ ./lx en_US | wc -l
  199019
$ ./lx en_US | awk -F'\t' '$3 == "fuck" || $3 == "table" || $3 == "Trump"'
00000000	00800002	fuck
00000000	00000000	table
00002000	02000081	Trump
```
The same thing in Swift, loading the functions at runtime with `dlopen` and `dlsym` so you don't need to link against
a private framework. It prints only words that carry one of the three tiers:

```
// lexflags.swift — swiftc -O lexflags.swift -o lexflags && ./lexflags en_US
import Foundation
let lexicon = dlopen("/System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/Lexicon.framework/Lexicon", RTLD_NOW)!
func sym<T>(_ name: String, as _: T.Type) -> T { unsafeBitCast(dlsym(lexicon, name)!, to: T.self) }
typealias LXRef = UnsafeRawPointer
let create     = sym("LXLexiconCreate", as: (@convention(c) (CFDictionary, UnsafeMutablePointer<Unmanaged<CFError>?>?) -> LXRef?).self)
let rootCursor = sym("LXLexiconCreateRootCursor", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> LXRef?).self)
let enumerate  = sym("LXCursorEnumerateEntriesRecursively", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef, @convention(block) (LXRef, UnsafeMutablePointer<Bool>) -> Void) -> Void).self)
let copyString = sym("LXEntryCopyString", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> Unmanaged<CFString>?).self)
let metaFlags  = sym("LXEntryGetMetaFlags", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> UInt32).self)
let category   = sym("LXEntryGetCategoryFlags", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> UInt32).self)
let localeKey  = dlsym(lexicon, "kLXLexiconLocaleKey")!.load(as: CFString.self)
let locale = CommandLine.arguments.dropFirst().first ?? "en_US"
guard let lex = create([localeKey: locale] as CFDictionary, nil), let root = rootCursor(lex) else {
    fatalError("could not open lexicon for \(locale)")
}
let tiers: [(UInt32, String)] = [(0x0080_0000, "vulgar"), (0x0100_0000, "offensive"), (0x0200_0000, "sensitive")]
enumerate(root) { entry, _ in
    let meta = metaFlags(entry)
    guard let tier = tiers.first(where: { meta & $0.0 != 0 })?.1,
          let word = copyString(entry)?.takeRetainedValue() else { return }
    print(tier, String(format: "%05x", category(entry)), word, separator: "\t")
}
```
Both are read-only. They open the same dictionary the keyboard uses and print it.

## 

Apple doesn't document these flags, so every meaning below is inferred: I grouped words by bit and read samples until
each group's theme was obvious. The system code helps with one of them. An enum case called
`offensiveVulgarSensitive` sits right next to the vulgar-word code, and three adjacent meta bits match it.

### 

| Bit | Tier | en\_US words | Examples | 
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x00800000` | vulgar | 1,050 | fuck, shit, cunt, cock, crap, wtf, fml, bullshitting, fucktard, shizzle, merde | 
| `0x01000000` | offensive | 663 | kike, wop, dago, fag, Paki, japs, Klansman, retard, Oriental, ass, asshole | 
| `0x02000000` | sensitive | 2,558 | damn, bitch, idiot, LSD, abortion, gun, suicide, anus, pee, poo | 

In en\_US a word has at most one tier: they never overlap. Out of 199,019 entries, 4,271 have one.

Roughly: **vulgar** is swearing and sex slang, **offensive** is slurs aimed at groups of people, and **sensitive** is
everything a keyboard shouldn't offer you unprompted: mild swears, insults, drugs, weapons, extremism, disease and
bodily functions.

### 

The other field is a topic bitmask, and a word can have several topics:

| Bit | Topic | en\_US words | Examples | 
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x00100` | excretion | 123 | feces, barf, crapper, piddle, pooped | 
| `0x00200` | body parts | 958 | nipples, navel, buttock, perineum, triceps | 
| `0x00400` | insults, identity-loaded | 823 | idiot, cretin, hick, pleb, sexist, homophobic, blacklist | 
| `0x00800` | disease | 93 | Covid, herpes, PTSD, leprosy, monkeypox | 
| `0x01000` | drugs | 222 | heroin, shroom, crackhead, hotbox, OD | 
| `0x02000` | politics, extremism | 266 | Hamas, Goebbels, Leninism, democrat, swastikas, Trump | 
| `0x04000` | religion, damnation | 420 | Sikhism, jihadi, Beelzebub, damn, hell, jeez | 
| `0x08000` | sex | 473 | nude, nookie, lecher, harlots, Pornhub, Hooters | 
| `0x10000` | violence, death | 373 | suicide, lynch, murders, hangings, slave, slaveholder | 
| `0x20000` | weapons, terrorism | 268 | AK-47, grenadier, jihad, sarin, kamikaze, yellowcake | 
| `0x40000` | catch-all "sensitive context" | 1,080 | God, Allah, Jews, gay, trans, bi, crazy, fat, ugly, sex, die | 

The topic flags and the tiers are independent. 2,052 English words have a topic but no tier: *gay*, *fat*, *God*,
*Allah* and *sex* are all tagged "sensitive context" but are not vulgar, offensive or sensitive. My guess is the topic
is a hint ("be careful how you rank this") and the tier is the rule.

The lower meta bits are dull: proper nouns, abbreviations, camel-case brand names like *iMac* and *tvOS*. Nothing to see
there.

## 

This is where it gets fun. Some flags are obviously right, and some made me laugh.

### 

- **Oedipus**: vulgar. Presumably because of *motherfucker*-adjacent jokes, or the complex. Sophocles would be thrilled.
- **reams**: vulgar. As in "to ream someone".
- **cooties**: vulgar. Your nine-year-old is swearing.
- **orgy**, **sext**, **merde**: fair enough.

### 

- **Tom** and **Mick**: offensive. *Uncle Tom* and the slur for Irish people, but also very common first names.
- **Oriental**: offensive.
- **papooses**: offensive.
- **conservatards**: offensive, the one political insult I found in the slur tier.
- **niggardly**: offensive. It means "stingy" and comes from Old Norse, unrelated to the slur. It has also caused [real controversies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Controversies_about_the_word_niggardly), which is presumably why
it's there.
- **ass** and **asshole**: offensive, not vulgar.

### 

- **pee** and **poo**: sensitive, with the excretion topic. So are *premenstrual*, *leprosy* and *herpesvirus*.
- **niggle** (a small worry, of Scandinavian origin) and **underling** (Old English for a subordinate) are sensitive and
share the insult topic. Similar words aren't flagged: *snigger* is clean but *niggle* is flagged, and *minion*, *lackey*, *flunky* and *stooge* are clean but *underling* is flagged. These look like hand-picked entries, not rules.
- **blacklist** and **whitelist** are sensitive with the insult/identity topic. That matches the industry move to *blocklist* and *allowlist*. Apple's own phrase-filter files are named `blocklist.dat`.
- **Braves** and **Chiefs** (team names with Native American mascots), **Londonderry** (the contested name for Derry), **Gentile**, **Jehovah**, **Mongol** and **Frenchier** are all sensitive.
- **Isis** is sensitive with the politics topic. Sorry to the Egyptian goddess.
- **slave**, **slavery** and **slaveholder** are sensitive with the violence topic.
- **idiot** is sensitive in English. Norwegian is stricter and puts *idiot* in the offensive tier.

## 

The sensitive tier has 109 capitalized words. Here is all of it:

Al-Qaeda, Al-Qaida, Aryan, Aryans, Auschwitz, Bacchus, Beelzebub, Birkenau, Brave(s), Buchenwald, Chief(s),
Chippendale(s), Christ-y, Christer(s), Crip(s), Dachau, Eichmann, Frenchier, Gentile(s), Gestapo(s), Goebbels,
Goering, Hamas, Hezbollah, Himmler, Hitler, Hitlerian, Hitlerism, Hitlerite(s), Hitlerjugend, Hooters, Isis,
Islamophobe(s), Islamophobic, Jehovah(s), Jewfro(s), Jezebel(s), Kalashnikov(s), Kristallnacht, Kuomintang,
Londonderry, Luftwaffe, Mao, Mauthausen, Mickie(s), Mollie(s), Mongol(s), Mossad, Nazi(s), Nazism, Osama, Pornhub,
Quaalude(s), Reich, Reichsmark, Reichstag, Sachsenhausen, Satan, Satanism, Shoah, Sinophobe(s), Sinophobic, Sodom,
Stasi, Taliban, Treblinka, **Trump, Trumps**, Unabomber, Uzi(s)


(Plurals and possessives folded for brevity.)

Every other real person on that list is dead, and nearly all of them are Nazi officials, dictators or terrorists. Then there's Trump:

```
category  meta      word
00002000  02000081  Trump        sensitive tier + politics topic
00002000  02000081  Trumps
00002000  02000081  Trump's
00000000  00000000  trump        (the card-game word: clean)
00000000  00000000  trumped
```
For comparison:

| Word | en\_US | 
|---|---|
| Trump | sensitive, politics topic | 
| Hitler | sensitive, politics topic | 
| Biden | clean | 
| Obama | clean | 
| Putin | clean | 
| Stalin | clean | 
| Musk | not in the dictionary | 

`en_GB` matches `en_US`. Other languages differ: the German dictionary has *Trump* clean (and puts *Hitler* in the
**offensive** tier), and Swedish is the one that flags *Putin* as sensitive.

What the flag *does* matters here. As far as I can tell, a sensitive word is one the keyboard shouldn't suggest on its
own. You can still type it and it won't be corrected away. Think "keep this out of the QuickType bar unless the user is
clearly heading there", which is a lot milder than a ban.

There is a plausible reason Apple would want that for one specific name. In February 2025, iPhone dictation briefly
showed "Trump" when people said "racist". It went viral, and Apple called it a
"[phonetic overlap](https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/apple-glitch-voice-to-text-trump-rcna193733)" in the speech model and
shipped a fix within a day
([9to5Mac](https://9to5mac.com/2025/02/25/iphone-trump-siri-racist-bug/)). The dictionary files on my Mac are from
July 2025. A rule that keeps the name out of unprompted suggestions would stop that kind of thing from happening
again through the keyboard. I can't prove that's why it's there, and I don't have an older dictionary to compare
against. But it fits.

### 

Because I'm Norwegian and had to check:

| Word | Topic | Tier | 
|---|---|---|
| FrP, Høyre, Venstre, Rødt, SV, KrF, MDG | politics | none | 
| Støre | politics | none | 
| Solberg, Erna, Sylvi | none | none | 
| Listhaug | n/a | not in the dictionary | 
| Breivik, Quisling, Hitler | none | sensitive | 

Every party gets the politics topic and none gets a tier. The only Norwegians in the sensitive tier are a mass murderer and a Nazi collaborator.

## 

The same three tiers exist in every European dictionary I tried, Cyrillic included. The counts are entries, not lemmas, so heavily inflected languages like Polish and Russian look much worse than they are: every case and conjugation of a swear word is a separate entry.

| Locale | Vulgar | Offensive | Sensitive | Notable | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| en\_US | 1,050 | 663 | 2,558 | *idiot* is sensitive | 
| en\_GB | 1,055 | 872 | 2,337 | *chav* is offensive; *chink* is filed as **vulgar**, not offensive | 
| nb\_NO | 2,393 | 1,324 | 6,446 | *idiot* is offensive | 
| da\_DK | 1,179 | 3,314 | 8,551 | *fjols* ("fool") is offensive | 
| sv\_SE | 637 | 1,247 | 16,193 | *idiot* is **vulgar**; *Putin* is sensitive | 
| fi\_FI | 569 | 872 | 47 | The entire sensitive tier is *kakka* ("poop"), *kakkakasa* ("pile of poop") and *saakeli* | 
| de\_DE | 3,218 | 3,518 | 9,446 | *Hitler* and *beknackt* ("daft") are offensive; *Trump* is clean | 
| nl\_NL | 57 | 1,180 | 3,805 | Only 57 vulgar words, but *kanker* ("cancer", the classic Dutch swear) is one | 
| fr\_FR | 2,151 | 262 | 5,562 | *boche* is offensive | 
| es\_ES | 3,931 | 313 | 13,431 | *sudacas* and *fachas* are offensive | 
| it\_IT | 3,886 | 377 | 6,543 | *terrone* is offensive, and so is *nazismi* | 
| pt\_BR | 1,590 | 1,891 | 3,332 | *machista* and *velhinhos* ("little old people") are offensive | 
| pl\_PL | 9,698 | 1,436 | 6,190 | The biggest vulgar tier here, mostly inflections ( *dupczysz*, *srasz*) | 
| ru\_RU | 10,821 | 3,239 | 24,721 | Same story: мат inflects a lot | 

The bits don't seem to mean the same thing everywhere. Arabic and Hebrew return hundreds of thousands of "sensitive" entries, so those dictionaries probably reuse the bits for something else, and I left them out. Korean, Catalan and Hungarian return nothing, and Japanese crashes my dumper.

Samples from Norwegian, since that's what I type in when I'm not typing English:

- **Vulgar:** faen, jævla, dritt, fitte, kuk, pule, pissehull, rævhull, pulekanin, kåt, *morrabrød*.
- **Offensive:** *idiot*, *sigøyner*, *kinamann*, *riskokers* (literally "rice cookers", a slur for Asians), plus the
Norwegian n-word.
- **Sensitive:** helvete, satan, homo, quisling, Breivik, skinhead, abortnekt, trusene ("the panties").

The tier words are mostly what you'd expect, but the edges are different in each language, and that is where the
human-edited parts show. Norwegian calls *idiot* offensive and English calls it sensitive. German thinks Hitler is a
slur.

## 

There is a second, separate filter. Every English language model has a `blocklist.bundle`, and there's a
`qp_blocklist.bundle` for QuickPath, the swipe keyboard:

```
/System/Library/LinguisticData/RequiredAssets_en.bundle/AssetData/en.lm/
├── blocklist.bundle/{blocklist.dat, blocklistidmap.dat}
└── qp_blocklist.bundle/{blocklist.dat, blocklistidmap.dat}
```
`blocklistidmap.dat` is a 20-byte header followed by `(lexicon token ID, class ID)` pairs of 32-bit integers. Mapping
the token IDs back through the dictionary gives 2,544 words in 930 classes. Most classes are inflection groups:

```
931   fuck | fucked | fucking | fucks
1181  molest | molestation | molested | molester | molesting
1514  died | dies | dying
1611  Holocaust | holocaust | holocausts
1614  denied | denies | deny | denying
923   Semite | Semites | Semitic
1487  ghetto | ghettoes | ghettos
1720  animals | brown | cats
```
`blocklist.dat` is a packed trie over those class IDs, so it blocks *sequences*: "deny" followed by "Holocaust", and
whatever 1720 pairs with. A class that puts *brown* next to *animals* and *cats* suggests the list targets specific
phrasings rather than single words, though which phrasings I can't tell without decoding the trie. The runtime check is `LMLanguageModelTokenSequenceIsBlocklisted` in
`LanguageModeling.framework`. I got far enough to learn that its fourth and fifth arguments include an output
pointer, but my probe still crashes intermittently, so I haven't read the actual phrases yet. That's for a follow-up.

## 

- **Meanings are inferred.** Apple documents none of these bits. The tier names come from an enum in the system code
and the topics from reading thousands of samples. Both are consistent, but they're still a reading.
- **Flagged is not censored.** As far as I can tell these flags decide what the keyboard volunteers, not what you can
type.
- **One machine.** Everything here comes from macOS 15.6 (24G84) with LinguisticData build 438 from July 2025. iOS and
other macOS versions may ship different dictionaries.
- **Private API.** The functions can change or disappear in any update. Don't ship this in an app.

## 

```
# Your own learned-swears database (probably empty on a Mac)
sqlite3 -readonly ~/Library/Keyboard/VulgarWordUsage.db 'select * from vword_usage'
# Build the Swift version from above and filter by tier
swiftc -O lexflags.swift -o lexflags
./lexflags en_US | awk -F'\t' '$1 == "vulgar" {print $3}' | sort -u | less
./lexflags nb_NO | awk -F'\t' '$3 == "faen" || $3 == "helvete" || $3 == "idiot"'
```
If you'd rather not build anything, the
[gist](https://gist.github.com/HelgeSverre/25d9e54a09533e84ada32c2bc26e560c) has every tiered word for 15 locales as
TSV, plus the code and a script that regenerates them. It's a snapshot of macOS 15.6 and won't be kept up to date.

If you find something funnier than *Oedipus*, I want to hear about it.

At the recent EMFCamp, I bumped in to Professor Kate Devlin who was talking a little about the AI Resist List. I think one of the useful things we can do is loudly complain about shitty uses of AI. Here's an example.
As mentioned in a previous post, I'm contacting companies which send malformed calendar invites. One of the organisation I contacted was the British online supermarket Ocado. They don't have an easy way to contact their technical team, and no obvious paths to raise a bug report, so I filled in their usual customer service feedback form. I included a clear statement of the problem and a detailed technical analysis of why I thought it was a problem with their service.
After sending in my message, I received this back from "Lulu" at Ocado:
						
Thanks for getting in touch and sharing this feedback about our calendar files.
You're entirely right—having a technical glitch pop up when you're trying to organise your delivery is a real pain, so I've made sure to pass your feedback on to our technical and webshop team.
We really appreciate you taking the time to help us improve our service. I hope you have a wonderful rest of your day
I mean, that's AI right? It starts with the classic tell of a sycophantic agreement.
Next up is the em-dash. Beloved by chatbots but almost unheard of in British English style guides.
Finally (and this is hard to quantify) it just doesn't feel like a customer service response. They're usually poorly spelled, have dodgy grammar, and ask a bunch of irrelevant questions. The message gave me no confidence that anyone had looked at the problem and I doubted it had been passed on to a technically competent human.
I immediately got a customer satisfaction survey. Usually I give top marks to humans because, even though Net Promoter Score is bullshit, I don't want customer service agents to suffer the indignity of a bad review. But in this survey I vented my spleen - giving crappy 1 ⭐ scores on every metric and complaining vociferously about how rude it is to use an AI to deal with a genuine complaint.
I was both surprised and delighted to receive this back a few days after my invective was sent:
						
I saw your survey comment about getting a robotic, AI-generated response previously, and I wanted to reach out personally to apologise. There is nothing more frustrating than pointing out a legitimate bug only to feel like you're talking to a brick wall. I promise you there is a real person typing this out!
Second, I wanted to send a massive thank you for the incredibly detailed diagnostic. It is rare to get feedback that tells us exactly what is broken and how to fix it.
I can assure you that this has been passed to our team to look into. Your feedback is going to make things much smoother for a lot of people, and we really appreciate you taking the extra time to help us get it right.
Thank you again, I do hope that this issue is resolved quickly. If there is anything else I can help with in the meantime, please don't hesitate to get in touch.
Perhaps I'm being touchingly naïve, but that feels a lot more human, right? The grammar isn't perfect, the sentences are a bit more rambly, and it appears to have actually engaged with the contents of my message.
I get that having a million irate customer service messages is a hassle. Using AI to triage them probably makes business sense, summarising the verbose ones could be useful for customer service agents, and totting up general themes is almost certainly a sensible way to gather metrics without overloading the workforce.
But using an AI to reply to a human is just disrespectful. It says the organisation values their customer's time at less than their own.
It's OK to call out shitty AI responses and insist that a human engages with you.

At the recent EMFCamp, I bumped in to [Professor Kate Devlin](https://www.kcl.ac.uk/people/kate-devlin) who was talking a little about the [AI Resist List](https://airesistlist.org/). I think one of the useful things we can do is loudly complain about shitty uses of AI. Here's an example.

As mentioned in a previous post, I'm [contacting companies which send malformed calendar invites](https://shkspr.mobi/blog/2026/07/google-calendar-unable-to-launch-event-caused-by-missing-dtstamp/). One of the organisation I contacted was the British online supermarket Ocado. They don't have an easy way to contact their technical team, and no obvious paths to raise a bug report, so I filled in their usual customer service feedback form. I included a clear statement of the problem and a detailed technical analysis of why I thought it was a problem with their service.

After sending in my message, I received this back from "Lulu" at Ocado:

Thanks for getting in touch and sharing this feedback about our calendar files.

You're entirely right—having a technical glitch pop up when you're trying to organise your delivery is a real pain, so I've made sure to pass your feedback on to our technical and webshop team.

We really appreciate you taking the time to help us improve our service. I hope you have a wonderful rest of your day


I mean, that's AI right? It starts with the classic tell of a [sycophantic agreement](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/3382).

Next up is the em-dash. [Beloved by chatbots](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/10/books/review/em-dash-chatbot-human-language.html) but almost unheard of in British English style guides.

Finally (and this is hard to quantify) it just doesn't *feel* like a customer service response. They're usually poorly spelled, have dodgy grammar, and ask a bunch of irrelevant questions. The message gave me no confidence that anyone had looked at the problem and I doubted it had been passed on to a technically competent human.

I immediately got a customer satisfaction survey. Usually I give top marks to humans because, even though [Net Promoter Score is bullshit](https://shkspr.mobi/blog/2024/01/whats-the-incentive-to-tell-the-truth-on-surveys/), I don't want customer service agents to suffer the indignity of a bad review. But in this survey I vented my spleen - giving crappy 1 ⭐ scores on every metric and complaining vociferously about how *rude* it is to use an AI to deal with a genuine complaint.

I was both surprised and delighted to receive this back a few days after my invective was sent:

I saw your survey comment about getting a robotic, AI-generated response previously, and I wanted to reach out personally to apologise. There is nothing more frustrating than pointing out a legitimate bug only to feel like you're talking to a brick wall. I promise you there is a real person typing this out!

Second, I wanted to send a massive thank you for the incredibly detailed diagnostic. It is rare to get feedback that tells us *exactly* what is broken and how to fix it.

I can assure you that this has been passed to our team to look into. Your feedback is going to make things much smoother for a lot of people, and we really appreciate you taking the extra time to help us get it right.

Thank you again, I do hope that this issue is resolved quickly. If there is anything else I can help with in the meantime, please don't hesitate to get in touch.


Perhaps I'm being touchingly naïve, but that *feels* a lot more human, right? The grammar isn't perfect, the sentences are a bit more rambly, and it appears to have actually engaged with the contents of my message.

I get that having a million irate customer service messages is a hassle. Using AI to triage them probably makes business sense, summarising the verbose ones could be useful for customer service agents, and totting up general themes is almost certainly a sensible way to gather metrics without overloading the workforce.

But using an AI to reply to a human is just disrespectful. It says the organisation values their customer's time at less than their own.

It's OK to call out shitty AI responses and insist that a human engages with you.

fields.text:
AI is destroying my CS degree
I am a computer science student. I got a scholarship to study computer science and AI last year and I love it! It's something that I wanted to do since I was a kid but couldn't afford it.
It's been a huge learning curve. I only had a B in maths from GCSE (which is the exam you take at 16 for non UK folk) and no technical training other than the funny little games I made on OpenProcessing*.
Regardless of how hard it's been, I have enjoyed the challenge. I wouldn't have signed up to study computing if I thought it would be an easy ride. The problem is that my university seems to be having an existential crisis because of AI, and it's making the experience much shittier than it was before.
The flip flopping makes everything uncertain
During my studies, my uni has flip flopped between YOU MUST NEVER USE AI and YOU MUST USE AI and also YES WE'RE USING AI BUT THAT DOESN'T MEAN YOU SHOULD!
They seem to have made an art of choosing the worst possible use cases for AI (marking and feedback, course content creation, and student engagement emails) and going all in on them, only to roll back the decision 3 months later. Students are mandated to use AI in assignments, only to reach the next module where you lose marks for even touching an LLM.
Coursework design has gone down the toilet
I mean, it was never perfect to begin with. Assessing skill in computer science is a difficult problem to solve, but getting Claude to crank out bloated assessment briefs is not the solution. Whereas before, assignments were designed by a person who thought them through at least once, then approved by other people in the department, now I doubt they're getting read more than once (if that). Errors abound, often with corrections coming a week or two before the deadline.
The amount of work involved has also tripled - LLMs don't know how much effort it takes for a student to learn new material then complete technical tasks, and professors are too far along in their careers to notice this when skim reading an AI generated brief. So those of us with less technical experience are forced to speed run content, which SUCKS! I am here to learn, god damn it, not barely scratch the surface of the 15 deliverables I have for a 3,000 word assignment.
Tutors are overloaded (even more than usual)
You know what university financiers love to hear? SCALE! Learning at scale, preferable automated, so they can milk the cash cow as much as possible without paying for extra staff. There has always been tension between educational and commercial interests in every institution, but the AI hype has forced through a level of workload that is unethical and unsustainable for tutors and lecturers. I only hear from my tutor these days when I haven't accessed the online portal in a while, because their data dashboard flagged me as 'at risk' T_T
Doomers left, right and centre
I don't care if computer science and maths are over! I still want to learn about them! OK, I do care about my future career, but it still doesn't mean I want to forget everything I learned or stop progressing on this journey. There are so many interesting avenues to explore (some AI, some not), but I can't move for headlines about how software engineering is over/not using AI makes you obsolete/blah blah blah. Can't a girl learn statistics for fun?
I could go on, but I won't. It'll give me indigestion. Maybe I'll go back to OpenProcessing for a bit and make some more silly games now I actually know how to do a bit of programming.

# AI is destroying my CS degree

                
            

I am a computer science student. I got a scholarship to study computer science and AI last year and I love it! It's something that I wanted to do since I was a kid but couldn't afford it.

It's been a huge learning curve. I only had a B in maths from GCSE (which is the exam you take at 16 for non UK folk) and no technical training other than the funny little games I made on OpenProcessing\*.

Regardless of how hard it's been, I have enjoyed the challenge. I wouldn't have signed up to study computing if I thought it would be an easy ride. The problem is that my university seems to be having an existential crisis because of AI, and it's making the experience much shittier than it was before.

### The flip flopping makes everything uncertain

During my studies, my uni has flip flopped between YOU MUST NEVER USE AI and YOU MUST USE AI and also YES WE'RE USING AI BUT THAT DOESN'T MEAN YOU SHOULD!

They seem to have made an art of choosing the worst possible use cases for AI (marking and feedback, course content creation, and student engagement emails) and going all in on them, only to roll back the decision 3 months later. Students are mandated to use AI in assignments, only to reach the next module where you lose marks for even touching an LLM.

### Coursework design has gone down the toilet

I mean, it was never perfect to begin with. Assessing skill in computer science is a difficult problem to solve, but getting Claude to crank out bloated assessment briefs is not the solution. Whereas before, assignments were designed by a person who thought them through at least once, then approved by other people in the department, now I doubt they're getting read more than once (if that). Errors abound, often with corrections coming a week or two before the deadline.

The amount of work involved has also tripled - LLMs don't know how much effort it takes for a student to learn new material then complete technical tasks, and professors are too far along in their careers to notice this when skim reading an AI generated brief. So those of us with less technical experience are forced to speed run content, which SUCKS! I am here to learn, god damn it, not barely scratch the surface of the 15 deliverables I have for a 3,000 word assignment.
